opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the specific technical skills matter less than they used to, and the meta-skills matter a lot more. If I were 25 right now, I'd focus on getting really good at learning new things quickly, because the tools are going to keep changing underneath you every year or two, and the people who do well will be the ones who adapt fastest rather than the ones who mastered one particular thing.

Related to that: get extremely fluent with AI tools. Not in a "learn prompt engineering" way, but in the sense of making them part of how you think and work every day, figuring out what they're great at, where they fall short, and how to get leverage from them. The gap between people who do that and people who don't is going to be enormous.

Beyond that, I'd say resilience, judgment, and taste. When generating things gets cheap, deciding what's actually worth doing, what's good, and what people really want becomes the scarce part. Being able to work with other people, understand what they need, and earn their trust also doesn't go away. If anything it gets more valuable.

And I'd encourage people to be a little bolder than feels comfortable. Those years are a great time to take swings, because the cost of being wrong is low and the world is about to have a lot of new openings in it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing, honestly, is to get really good at using these tools. Not in a superficial way, but to actually sit down and figure out what the models can do, where they fall apart, how to get a lot of leverage out of them. The people who are going to do incredibly well over the next couple of decades are the ones who treat AI as something that multiplies what they can do, rather than something that happens to them.

Beyond that, I'd say the meta-skills matter more than any specific technical skill. Learning how to learn quickly. Figuring out what you actually want and being willing to go after it. Resilience, because things are going to change a lot and you're going to be wrong about stuff. Creativity, taste, judgment about what's worth doing, those become more valuable, not less, when the cost of execution drops.

And I'd push back a little on the premise that you need to predict exactly what the world looks like in twenty years. You don't. Nobody does. What you can do is build a kind of adaptability so that whatever the world ends up looking like, you can find your footing fast. Spend time with smart, ambitious people. Work on hard problems. Stay curious. If I had to bet on one thing, it's that the ability to have an idea and actually make it happen, to go from zero to something real, is going to be the most rewarded skill there is.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important skill is learning how to learn. It’s hard to predict which specific technical skills will matter in twenty years, but being able to pick up something new, get good at it, and adapt when the world changes seems pretty durable.

I’d also get comfortable using AI tools. Try building something with them, see where they help and where they fail, and develop your own judgment about the results. There’s a lot you learn through that process that you won’t learn just by reading about it.

And then there are the human skills: communicating clearly, understanding what other people need, working well with a team, deciding what’s worth doing. As it gets easier to execute on an idea, choosing the right idea becomes more important.

At twenty-five, I’d give myself room to experiment. Do things, get feedback, change your mind. Being able to act under uncertainty is useful, because you’re probably not going to get a perfect map of what comes next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important skill is learning how to learn. The tools are going to change, the jobs are going to change, and being able to get good at something new quickly will matter a lot.

I’d also focus on figuring out what questions to ask. When you can get help producing almost anything, judgment becomes really valuable: What’s worth doing? What does a good result look like? How do you know whether an answer is right?

And then agency—getting comfortable taking an idea and actually making it happen. Try things, ask for feedback, recover when something doesn’t work. Build the habit of moving forward without needing someone to give you a perfectly specified task.

You should learn to use AI tools well, of course. But I wouldn’t organize your whole education around mastering one particular tool. Use them to build things you care about. You’ll learn the technology, and you’ll also develop taste, persistence, and an understanding of what people actually need.
